title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about building a revision strategy rather than simply starting to revise. By the end you will be able to build a strategy around your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge. You will be able to apply active-learning principles so your revision tests you rather than just reminding you. You will also be able to select technique families, visual, auditory or kinaesthetic, to match your material.

None of this assumes you already revise well. It assumes you want your revision time to do more than it currently does, and shows you how to connect the pieces so it does.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: build a revision strategy around your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge
apply active-learning principles to your revision, distinguishing active techniques from passive review
select active revision techniques across visual, auditory and kinaesthetic approaches to fit your material

title: Signpost
body: The course has four short lessons. First, the two building blocks of a revision strategy: your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge. Second, what makes revision active rather than passive. Third, matching technique families, visual, auditory and kinaesthetic, to your material. Fourth, bringing strategy, active technique and material together so you revise on purpose rather than by habit. Work through them in order; the last lesson depends on the first three.
instruction: Work through the four lessons in order.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: Orientation
body: By this point you have probably already revised for more than one set of exams, with mixed results. This lesson looks at what a revision strategy is actually built from: your use of time, and your ability to spot the gaps in what you know. Once those two pieces are in view, planning your next round of revision stops being guesswork.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not starting from nothing here. The aim at this stage is to turn revision you already do into something closer to a strategy: deliberate about where your time goes, and honest about what you do not yet know, rather than a routine you repeat because it is familiar.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: identify the two elements an effective revision strategy is built on: your use of time and your ability to spot gaps in your knowledge
recognise, in a worked example, how a student turns a vague plan into a strategy built on time and gaps
apply the stages of a revision strategy to plan your own revision for a module in {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body:
A revision strategy is more than a timetable. It rests on two things working together: how you allocate the time you have, and how accurately you can identify the gaps between what you already know and what the exam will actually ask of you. Time allocated without an honest view of the gaps produces a schedule that still revises the wrong material for too long.

Gaps identified without a plan for your time stay as observations rather than becoming a strategy. A strategy exists where the two meet: time deliberately allocated to the gaps that matter most, reviewed and adjusted as your knowledge changes.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about how you revised for your last set of exams. Did you allocate your time according to where your knowledge was thinnest, or spread it evenly across everything regardless of need? What would you do differently next time?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A revision strategy is built from two things working together: your use of time, and an honest, tested view of the gaps in your knowledge. You can now identify those two building blocks, recognise a plan that is built on them rather than on habit, and apply the stages, audit, identify, allocate, monitor, to a module of your own. The next lesson looks at what makes the revision you then do active rather than passive.

title: Orientation
body: Most students have, at some point, mistaken re-reading for revising. This lesson looks at what actually separates active revision from passive review, and why that distinction matters more than which particular technique you happen to reach for first.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not being asked to abandon everything you currently do. You are being asked to apply active-learning principles across your modules more consistently, rather than falling back on passive review whenever time is short or the material feels dense.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: distinguish active revision techniques from passive review
recognise, in a worked example, the active move a student makes instead of re-reading passively
replace a passive revision habit of your own with an active technique in {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body:
Active revision asks you to retrieve or reconstruct knowledge without the source in front of you, through self-testing, explaining a concept aloud from memory, or solving a problem cold. Passive review, by contrast, puts the source in front of you and asks you to recognise it: re-reading notes, highlighting a textbook, or replaying a lecture recording.

Passive review feels productive precisely because recognition is easy, and that ease is its problem: it builds a sense of familiarity that does not survive contact with an exam question, where recognising material is not what is being asked for.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a revision session you have actually sat through. How much of it, honestly, was re-reading or highlighting rather than testing yourself or reconstructing something from memory? What is one passive habit you could swap for an active one?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Active revision retrieves knowledge without the source in front of you; passive review keeps the source visible and asks only for recognition. You can now distinguish the two, recognise the active move a student makes instead of re-reading, and replace at least one passive habit of your own with an active technique. The next lesson looks at how to choose which active technique actually fits the material you are revising.

title: Orientation
body: Not every active technique suits every topic. This lesson looks at three broad families of active revision technique, visual, auditory and kinaesthetic, and at how to match one to the material in front of you rather than reaching for a single favourite regardless of fit.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You likely already lean on one technique more than the others, and that is a reasonable starting point. At this stage the expectation is to apply more than one family across your modules, choosing deliberately rather than defaulting to whichever feels most comfortable.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: describe the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families of active revision technique and match a technique to its family
recognise, in a worked example, how a student selects techniques to fit the material
select active techniques that fit the material you are revising in {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body:
Active revision techniques fall loosely into three families. Visual techniques turn material into diagrams, flowcharts or concept maps that show how its parts connect. Auditory techniques use speech: explaining a concept aloud, teaching it to someone else, or recording and listening back, to test whether you can produce it in your own words.

Kinaesthetic techniques involve doing something physical with the material: working through a problem by hand, building a model, or rehearsing a process step by step. None of the three families is superior in general; each tends to fit some kinds of material better than others.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the technique you default to when you revise, whatever the material. Does it actually fit everything you use it for, or does it just happen to be the one you reach for first? Which topic in your own studies might suit a different family altogether?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Active revision techniques fall into three families, visual, auditory and kinaesthetic, each with its own defining move, and none of them superior in general. You can now describe the three families, recognise a student matching technique to material rather than defaulting to one favourite, and select a technique that fits what you are actually revising. The final lesson brings strategy, active revision and technique choice together into one practice.

title: Orientation
body: The first three lessons looked at a revision strategy, active revision, and matching technique to material as three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together: one way of revising on purpose, where strategy, technique and material stay connected, rather than running as three unrelated jobs.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You have already met each of the three pieces on their own. The expectation now is to connect them across a whole module, so that your use of time, your choice of technique and the material in front of you inform each other, rather than sitting in separate parts of your routine.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect your use of time and your knowledge gaps to the stage of a revision strategy they inform
connect a stage of a revision strategy to the active technique it calls for, rather than passive review
apply a revision strategy, active revision and well-matched techniques together as one practice across your own studies

title: Concept: definition
body:
Revising on purpose means keeping three things connected rather than treating them as separate jobs: a strategy that allocates your time to the gaps in your knowledge, revision that is active rather than passive, and a technique chosen to fit the material at hand. Dropping any one connection weakens the other two.

A strategy without active technique still produces passive review on schedule. Active technique applied without regard to the material wastes effort on a poor fit. The three only work as a system when each stage of the strategy calls on an active technique suited to what is actually being revised.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look at your revision plan for the module you find hardest right now. Where does it show a stage of your strategy actually connected to an active technique that fits the material, and where does it not yet? What would make it feel like one plan rather than three separate jobs?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Revising on purpose means keeping a strategy, active revision and a well-matched technique connected, rather than running them as three separate jobs. You can now connect your use of time and your knowledge gaps to the stage of a strategy they inform, connect that stage to the active technique it calls for, and apply all three together across your own studies. That completes the course; the final test checks all three course outcomes together.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Building a strategy, stage by stage
body: Open each stage below to see what it involves.
instruction: Select a heading to open it.

_items.title: Audit what you already know
_items.body: Before you allocate a single hour, work out what you can already do without notes. This stage is honest stock-taking, not revision itself.

_items.title: Identify the gaps
_items.body: Compare that audit against what the module actually requires. The distance between the two is where your strategy needs to spend its effort.

_items.title: Allocate time to the gaps that matter
_items.body: Give the largest share of your available time to the gaps most likely to appear in the exam, not to the topics you already find comfortable.

_items.title: Monitor and adjust as you go
_items.body: Revisit the audit regularly. A gap you close stops needing time; a gap that resists closing needs more, or a different technique.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students sit down in the same week to plan revision for the same module.

{{learner-a}} opens a blank weekly planner and splits the available hours evenly across every topic on the module outline, on the basis that this feels fair and covers everything. By the end of the first week, the plan is already behind: some topics took longer than their allotted slot, others needed almost none of it, and the schedule gives no way to tell which was which.

{{learner-b}} starts the same week by working through a set of past short-answer questions without notes, marking which ones they could answer confidently and which exposed a genuine gap. Only then do they build the weekly planner, weighting the hours toward the topics the audit flagged as weak, and leaving the strongest topics a single short review session near the end.

Both students have the same number of hours. Only {{learner-b}}'s plan is built on an honest view of where those hours are actually needed.

title: Building your own strategy
displayTitle: How to do it
body: Use these questions to start building a revision strategy for a module in {{context}}, before you commit a single hour to a timetable.
instruction: Tick each item once you have thought it through.

_items.text: Have I tested myself without notes to see what I can already do?
Have I compared that against what the module will actually ask of me?
Have I weighted my available time toward the gaps that showed up, rather than splitting it evenly?
Have I left room to revisit the audit and adjust the plan partway through?
Could I explain, in one sentence, why my current plan gives more time to some topics than others?

title: Formative check: what a revision strategy is built from
displayTitle: What does an effective revision strategy need, beyond the time you make available for it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does an effective revision strategy need beyond available time?

_items.text: An honest, tested view of where the gaps in your knowledge actually are.
_items.feedback: Yes. Time without that view still gets spent on the wrong material.

_items.text: A planner app with a more attractive layout.
_items.feedback: The format of the planner is not what makes a strategy effective.

_items.text: A guarantee that every topic gets exactly equal time.
_items.feedback: Equal time ignores the fact that some topics need more than others.

_items.text: A longer list of topics to cover in the same number of hours.
_items.feedback: Adding topics does not address how the time already available is allocated.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Time only becomes a strategy once it is pointed at genuine gaps.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what turns a timetable into a strategy, rather than just a list of hours.
_incorrect.final: An effective strategy needs an honest, tested view of where the gaps actually are. The other options describe things that do not make a plan more effective.

title: Formative check: what the second student's audit changed
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did testing herself without notes let the second student do that the first student could not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the audit let the second student do differently?

_items.text: Weight the available hours toward the topics that actually needed them.
_items.feedback: Yes. The audit told her where the hours would do the most good.

_items.text: Finish the plan more quickly than the first student.
_items.feedback: Speed of planning is not what the worked example compares.

_items.text: Avoid revising some topics on the module outline altogether.
_items.feedback: The worked example does not describe skipping topics, only weighting time differently.

_items.text: Guarantee that every topic would be fully learned by the end of the week.
_items.feedback: An audit improves allocation; it does not guarantee complete mastery.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Testing herself first told her where the hours were actually needed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the audit specifically allowed her to do with her time.
_incorrect.final: The audit let the second student weight her hours toward the genuine gaps it revealed. The other options describe things the worked example does not show.

title: Formative check: applying the two building blocks
displayTitle: You are about to plan revision for a module in {{context}}. Which first step best reflects this lesson?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the best first step when planning revision for a module?

_items.text: Test yourself without notes to find the genuine gaps, then allocate time to them.
_items.feedback: Yes. Starting from a tested view of the gaps is what the lesson has set out.

_items.text: Split the available hours evenly across every topic on the outline.
_items.feedback: Even splitting ignores the fact that some topics need more time than others.

_items.text: Start with whichever topic feels most comfortable, to build confidence first.
_items.feedback: Comfort is not the same as need; this risks giving time to topics that need it least.

_items.text: Write a timetable before deciding what any of the time is for.
_items.feedback: A timetable built before the gaps are known still risks revising the wrong material.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A tested audit of the gaps, followed by time allocated to them, is the strategy this lesson has described.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which step this lesson places before the timetable itself.
_incorrect.final: The strongest first step is to test yourself for the genuine gaps and then allocate time to them in {{context}}. The other options skip or reverse that order.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The same material, revised two ways
body: Three pairs contrasting a passive move with its active counterpart.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Re-reading
_items.subtitle: vs. self-testing
_items.text: Reading your notes again confirms they still make sense to you. Testing yourself without them confirms whether you can produce the content unaided.

_items.title: Highlighting
_items.subtitle: vs. explaining aloud
_items.text: Highlighting marks what looks important. Explaining the same idea aloud, from memory, exposes exactly where your understanding runs out.

_items.title: Watching again
_items.subtitle: vs. recalling cold
_items.text: Replaying a lecture recording feels thorough but asks nothing of you. Recalling the same content cold, before checking, is what actually tests whether it has stuck.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students are revising the same dense topic the week before an exam.

{{learner-a}} spends the evening reading back through a full set of lecture notes twice, underlining the sentences that seem most important. By the end, the material feels familiar, and {{learner-a}} closes the notes satisfied that the evening has been well spent.

{{learner-b}} closes the notes first, then tries to write out the topic's main argument from memory, checking only afterwards against the original. The attempt is patchy in places, which is uncomfortable, but it shows exactly which parts of the argument {{learner-b}} can reconstruct unaided and which still need work.

Both students spend the same evening on the same topic. Only {{learner-b}} finishes it knowing which parts of the knowledge are actually secure.

title: Making a revision session active
displayTitle: How to do it
body: Use these questions to check whether a revision session in {{context}} is active or passive before you start it.
instruction: Tick each item once you have thought it through.

_items.text: Have I closed the source material before trying to recall anything?
Am I producing an answer, explanation or working, rather than just recognising one?
Have I checked my attempt against the source only after making it, not before?
Have I noticed where the attempt was patchy, rather than skipping past it?
Could I describe, in one sentence, what this session asked me to do that re-reading would not?

title: Formative check: what distinguishes active revision
displayTitle: What is the key difference between an active revision technique and a passive one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What distinguishes active revision from passive review?

_items.text: Active revision asks you to retrieve knowledge without the source in front of you; passive review keeps the source visible.
_items.feedback: Yes. Retrieval without the source is what makes a technique active.

_items.text: Active revision always takes longer to complete than passive review.
_items.feedback: Duration is not what separates the two; a short self-test can still be active.

_items.text: Active revision only works for essay-based subjects.
_items.feedback: The active/passive distinction applies across subjects, not to one kind of content.

_items.text: Active revision means revising with other people in the room.
_items.feedback: Working with others can help, but it is not what makes a technique active or passive.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Removing the source and retrieving the knowledge yourself is what makes revision active.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about whether the source is visible while you are working, not how long the session takes.
_incorrect.final: Active revision removes the source and asks you to retrieve the knowledge yourself; passive review keeps the source in view. The other options describe things that do not define the distinction.

title: Formative check: why the second student's evening was uncomfortable
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the second student's attempt feel patchy in places?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the second student's recall attempt feel patchy?

_items.text: Because trying to recall the argument unaided exposed parts that were not yet secure.
_items.feedback: Yes. The discomfort was the attempt revealing a genuine gap, not a failure.

_items.text: Because the lecture notes themselves were incomplete.
_items.feedback: The worked example does not say the notes were missing anything.

_items.text: Because the student had not attended the lecture.
_items.feedback: Nothing in the worked example suggests the student missed the lecture.

_items.text: Because recalling from memory is always less accurate than re-reading.
_items.feedback: The discomfort reflects what was not yet learned, not a general flaw in recall.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The patchiness showed exactly which parts of the argument still needed work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the discomfort of recalling unaided actually revealed.
_incorrect.final: The attempt felt patchy because it exposed genuine gaps in what had been learned so far. The other options are not supported by the worked example.

title: Formative check: swapping a passive habit
displayTitle: You usually revise for {{context}} by re-reading your notes. Which change would make the session active instead?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which change makes a re-reading session active instead?

_items.text: Close the notes and try to write out the argument from memory before checking them.
_items.feedback: Yes. Closing the source and retrieving the content is what makes the session active.

_items.text: Re-read the notes a third time to be thorough.
_items.feedback: Repeating the same passive move does not change what the session is testing.

_items.text: Highlight the notes in a different colour.
_items.feedback: Highlighting remains a recognition task regardless of the colour used.

_items.text: Read the notes more slowly than before.
_items.feedback: Slowing down a passive technique does not make it active.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Closing the notes and attempting recall is what turns the session active.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that removes the source before you try to produce anything.
_incorrect.final: Closing the notes and writing the argument from memory in {{context}}, before checking, is what makes the session active. The other options keep the source visible throughout.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Three families, three defining moves
body: Open each family below to see its defining move and a short example.
instruction: Select a heading to open it.

_items.title: Visual
_items.body: Defining move: turning relationships into a diagram. A concept map of how several theories relate, or a flowchart of a multi-step process, suits material that is mainly about structure and connection.

_items.title: Auditory
_items.body: Defining move: producing the material in speech. Explaining a concept aloud to someone else, or teaching it from memory, suits material that is mainly about argument, reasoning or explanation.

_items.title: Kinaesthetic
_items.body: Defining move: doing the material physically. Working a calculation by hand repeatedly, or rehearsing a procedure step by step, suits material that is mainly about method or sequence.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students are each revising two very different topics on the same module: one about the structural relationships between several theories, the other a multi-step calculation method.

{{learner-a}} has always found concept maps useful, so both topics get the same treatment: a diagram of the theories, and a diagram of the calculation steps. The theory map works well, but the calculation diagram leaves {{learner-a}} able to describe the steps without being able to actually perform the calculation under pressure.

{{learner-b}} starts by asking what each topic is mainly testing. For the theories, a concept map showing how they relate. For the calculation, repeated practice working through it by hand until the sequence is automatic. The second topic gets a kinaesthetic technique instead of a visual one, because that is what the material actually calls for.

Both students use a technique they already know well. Only {{learner-b}} chooses which one to use based on what each topic needs.

title: Matching technique to material
displayTitle: How to do it
body: Use these questions to choose an active technique for a topic in {{context}}, rather than defaulting to the one you know best.
instruction: Tick each item once you have thought it through.

_items.text: Have I identified whether this topic is mainly about structure, argument or method?
Have I considered a visual, auditory and kinaesthetic option before choosing one?
Have I checked whether my usual technique actually fits this particular topic?
Have I tried the chosen technique on a small part of the topic before committing more time to it?
Could I explain, in one sentence, why this technique suits this material?

title: Formative check: identifying the three families
displayTitle: A technique that involves teaching a concept aloud to someone else, from memory, belongs to which family of active revision technique?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which family does explaining a concept aloud belong to?

_items.text: Auditory, because it produces the material in speech.
_items.feedback: Yes. Producing the content aloud is the defining move of the auditory family.

_items.text: Visual, because it can be written down afterwards.
_items.feedback: Writing it down afterwards is a separate step, not what defines the technique.

_items.text: Kinaesthetic, because speaking involves physical movement of the mouth.
_items.feedback: This stretches the physical element too far; the defining move is producing speech, not movement.

_items.text: None of the three families, because explaining is not really revision.
_items.feedback: Explaining a concept from memory is a clear example of active revision.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Explaining aloud from memory is a defining example of the auditory family.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the technique mainly asks you to produce: speech, a diagram, or a physical action.
_incorrect.final: Explaining a concept aloud from memory belongs to the auditory family, because it asks you to produce the material in speech. The other options misidentify what the technique mainly involves.

title: Formative check: why the calculation diagram did not work
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did a concept map of the calculation steps leave the first student unable to perform the calculation under pressure?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the diagram fail to prepare the student for the calculation?

_items.text: Because the calculation needed repeated hands-on practice, not a diagram of its steps.
_items.feedback: Yes. The material called for a kinaesthetic technique, which a diagram does not provide.

_items.text: Because the student drew the diagram incorrectly.
_items.feedback: The worked example does not suggest the diagram itself was wrong.

_items.text: Because concept maps never help with any kind of exam question.
_items.feedback: Concept maps worked well for the theory topic in the same example.

_items.text: Because the student did not spend enough time on the diagram.
_items.feedback: The issue was the type of technique, not the amount of time spent on it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A diagram describes the steps; it does not build the hands-on fluency the calculation needed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what kind of practice a calculation actually requires, compared with what a diagram provides.
_incorrect.final: The calculation needed repeated kinaesthetic practice, which a visual diagram of the steps does not supply. The other options are not supported by the worked example.

title: Formative check: choosing a technique for your own material
displayTitle: You are revising a topic in {{context}} that is mainly about following a multi-step method. Which family of technique is most likely to fit it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which family best fits material that is mainly about a multi-step method?

_items.text: Kinaesthetic, because repeated hands-on practice builds fluency with a method.
_items.feedback: Yes. A method is best secured by doing it repeatedly, which is the kinaesthetic family's defining move.

_items.text: Visual, because any method can be turned into a diagram.
_items.feedback: A diagram can describe a method but does not build the fluency that performing it provides.

_items.text: Auditory, because explaining a method aloud is the same as being able to perform it.
_items.feedback: Being able to describe a method is not the same as being able to execute it.

_items.text: Whichever family feels most familiar, regardless of the material.
_items.feedback: This lesson has shown that fit to the material, not familiarity, should guide the choice.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A method-heavy topic is best matched to a kinaesthetic technique, built through repeated practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which family's defining move actually builds fluency with a sequence of steps.
_incorrect.final: Material that is mainly about a multi-step method fits the kinaesthetic family, through repeated hands-on practice. The other options describe techniques that do not build that fluency.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Connecting strategy to technique
body: Three stages of a revision strategy, each connected to the active technique it calls for.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Auditing what you know
_items.subtitle: calls for self-testing
_items.text: Finding the gaps is itself an active technique: testing yourself without notes, not just listing topics you feel unsure about.

_items.title: Allocating time to the gaps
_items.subtitle: calls for repeated active sessions
_items.text: Once a gap is identified, the hours allocated to it need to be spent retrieving and reconstructing the material, not re-reading it again.

_items.title: Choosing a technique for the material
_items.subtitle: calls for a matched family
_items.text: The hours allocated to a gap do the most good when the technique used in them, visual, auditory or kinaesthetic, actually fits what that material is testing.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students plan their revision for a module with several distinct topics across a full term.

{{learner-a}} builds a timetable that allocates time sensibly, then revises each topic by re-reading the relevant notes, using whichever technique comes to mind first for each one. The strategy, the activity, and the choice of technique never quite line up: the plan looks organised, but much of the time inside it is still spent passively, on techniques chosen without reference to the material.

{{learner-b}} starts the same term by auditing what is already known, then allocates time to the gaps that audit reveals. For each gap, {{learner-b}} chooses an active technique, self-testing, explaining aloud, or working a method by hand, based on what that specific topic is mainly testing, and revisits the audit partway through to adjust both the time and the technique.

Both students have a plan for the term. Only {{learner-b}}'s plan keeps strategy, active revision and technique choice working as one connected practice throughout.

title: Checking your plan is connected
displayTitle: How to do it
body: Use these questions to check whether your revision plan for {{context}} keeps strategy, technique and material connected, rather than running as three separate jobs.
instruction: Tick each item once you have thought it through.

_items.text: Does my plan allocate time based on a tested audit of the gaps, not just an even split?
Is the time allocated to each gap actually spent retrieving the material, rather than re-reading it?
Have I chosen a technique for each topic based on what that topic is testing, rather than habit?
Do I revisit the plan partway through to adjust both the time and the technique?
Could I explain, in one sentence, how my strategy, my revision and my technique choices connect for one topic?

title: Formative check: why the three elements need to stay connected
displayTitle: Why does revising on purpose require a strategy, active revision and technique choice to stay connected, rather than being handled separately?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why must the three elements stay connected rather than separate?

_items.text: Because dropping any one connection weakens the other two, even if each element looks fine on its own.
_items.feedback: Yes. A strategy, activity and technique only work as a system when they inform each other.

_items.text: Because only one of the three elements actually affects your results.
_items.feedback: This lesson has shown that all three contribute; none can be dropped without cost.

_items.text: Because connecting them removes the need to revise at all.
_items.feedback: Connecting the three supports revision; it does not replace the need to do it.

_items.text: Because a strategy and a technique are actually the same thing.
_items.feedback: Lessons 1 and 3 treated strategy and technique as distinct, connected ideas, not identical ones.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Strategy, active revision and technique choice only work fully when each informs the others.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what happens to the other two elements when one of the three is handled in isolation.
_incorrect.final: Dropping any one connection weakens the system as a whole, even if the remaining pieces look fine alone. The other options misstate what this lesson has shown.

title: Formative check: a student revises a technical topic
displayTitle: A student audits a technical topic, finds a clear gap, and allocates two hours to it. Which next step keeps the plan connected, rather than letting it fall back into passive review?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which next step keeps the plan connected after allocating time?

_items.text: Choose an active technique, such as working the method by hand, that fits what the topic is testing.
_items.feedback: Yes. The allocated time still needs an active, well-matched technique to avoid becoming passive review.

_items.text: Spend the two hours re-reading the relevant notes a second time.
_items.feedback: Re-reading is passive; it would break the connection the plan depends on.

_items.text: Reduce the two hours, since the gap has already been identified.
_items.feedback: Identifying a gap does not close it; the allocated time is still needed.

_items.text: Move straight to a different topic, since this one has already been audited.
_items.feedback: Auditing a gap is the first step, not a reason to skip revising it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The allocated time still needs an active technique matched to the material to stay connected.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what would turn the allocated two hours back into passive review.
_incorrect.final: Choosing a matched active technique for the allocated time keeps the strategy, activity and material connected. The other options would break that connection.

title: Formative check: applying the connected practice to your own studies
displayTitle: You want to apply what this lesson has covered to your own revision in {{context}}. What should your plan do first?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should a connected revision plan do first?

_items.text: Audit what you already know, so the time you allocate afterwards goes to genuine gaps.
_items.feedback: Yes. The connected practice starts from an honest audit, before time or technique are decided.

_items.text: Choose your favourite technique and apply it to every topic from the start.
_items.feedback: This lesson has shown that technique choice should follow from what each topic needs, not come first.

_items.text: Build a detailed timetable before deciding what any of the time is for.
_items.feedback: A timetable built before the gaps are known risks repeating the disconnected plan in the worked example.

_items.text: Wait until closer to the exam before thinking about any of this.
_items.feedback: Delaying the audit leaves less time to allocate once the gaps are finally identified.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Starting from an honest audit is what keeps the rest of the plan, time and technique, properly connected.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think back to which step the worked example's stronger student took before anything else.
_incorrect.final: A connected plan starts from an audit of what you already know in {{context}}, so time and technique can follow from genuine gaps. The other options skip or reverse that order.

displayTitle: Why does a revision strategy need to account for the gaps in your knowledge, not just the time you have available?
body: Why does a revision strategy need to account for the gaps in your knowledge, not just the time you have available?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does a strategy need to account for knowledge gaps, not just time?

_items.text: Because time spent without regard to the gaps can still be spent on the wrong material.
_items.feedback: Yes. Time only becomes a strategy once it is pointed at genuine gaps.

_items.text: Because knowledge gaps close automatically once a timetable exists.
_items.feedback: A timetable alone does not close any gaps.

_items.text: Because exams never test material you already know well.
_items.feedback: Exams can test material you already know as well as material you do not.

_items.text: Because gaps in knowledge only matter in the final week before an exam.
_items.feedback: Gaps matter throughout revision, not only at the end.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A strategy needs both time and a genuine view of the gaps to be effective.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what happens to time that ignores where the gaps actually are.

displayTitle: What is the risk of allocating revision time evenly across every topic regardless of how well you already know it?
body: What is the risk of allocating revision time evenly across every topic regardless of how well you already know it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the risk of allocating time evenly regardless of prior knowledge?

_items.text: Topics you already know well take time away from topics with genuine gaps.
_items.feedback: Yes. Even allocation does not direct time toward where it is actually needed.

_items.text: It guarantees every topic will be learned to the same standard.
_items.feedback: Equal time does not guarantee equal mastery, since starting points differ.

_items.text: It removes the need to test yourself before revising.
_items.feedback: An even split does not remove the value of testing yourself first.

_items.text: It has no effect on how a revision strategy performs.
_items.feedback: Even allocation does affect performance, by under-serving genuine gaps.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Even allocation risks giving time to topics that need it least.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what an even split fails to take into account.

displayTitle: What distinguishes an active revision technique from a passive one?
body: What distinguishes an active revision technique from a passive one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What distinguishes active revision from passive review?

_items.text: An active technique retrieves knowledge without the source in front of you; a passive one keeps the source visible.
_items.feedback: Yes. Retrieval without the source is the defining feature of an active technique.

_items.text: An active technique always takes less time than a passive one.
_items.feedback: Duration does not distinguish the two; a brief self-test is still active.

_items.text: A passive technique is always more enjoyable to carry out.
_items.feedback: Enjoyment is not what separates active revision from passive review.

_items.text: An active technique requires revising with other people present.
_items.feedback: Working with others can help, but it does not define an active technique.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Removing the source and retrieving the knowledge yourself is what makes a technique active.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about whether the source is visible while the technique is being carried out.

displayTitle: Why does re-reading notes tend to create a false sense of how well material has been learned?
body: Why does re-reading notes tend to create a false sense of how well material has been learned?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does re-reading create a false sense of how well material is learned?

_items.text: Because recognising material while reading it is easier than producing it unaided.
_items.feedback: Yes. Recognition is a weaker test than retrieval, so it overstates how secure the knowledge is.

_items.text: Because re-reading always introduces new errors into your notes.
_items.feedback: Re-reading does not typically introduce errors; the issue is what it fails to test.

_items.text: Because notes become less accurate the more times they are read.
_items.feedback: The accuracy of notes does not change simply through repeated reading.

_items.text: Because re-reading takes longer than any other revision technique.
_items.feedback: Duration is not the reason re-reading misleads you about your learning.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Recognition feels like knowledge, but it is a weaker test than retrieving the material unaided.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what re-reading actually tests, compared with producing the material from memory.

displayTitle: Why might a single favourite revision technique fail to suit every topic in a module?
body: Why might a single favourite revision technique fail to suit every topic in a module?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why might one favourite technique fail to suit every topic?

_items.text: Because different topics are mainly about structure, argument or method, and each is served by a different family of technique.
_items.feedback: Yes. A technique's fit depends on what kind of material it is being used on.

_items.text: Because every technique becomes less effective the more often it is used.
_items.feedback: A technique's effectiveness depends on fit to the material, not on frequency of use alone.

_items.text: Because only one technique family is ever genuinely active.
_items.feedback: Visual, auditory and kinaesthetic techniques can all be active, depending on how they are used.

_items.text: Because favourite techniques are always chosen at random.
_items.feedback: A favourite technique is usually chosen through familiarity, not at random.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Different topics call for different families of technique, so one favourite rarely fits all of them.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what actually varies between topics that a single technique might not account for.

displayTitle: What should mainly guide the choice between a visual, auditory or kinaesthetic technique for a given topic?
body: What should mainly guide the choice between a visual, auditory or kinaesthetic technique for a given topic?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should mainly guide the choice of technique for a topic?

_items.text: What the topic itself is mainly testing: structure, argument or method.
_items.feedback: Yes. Matching the technique to what the material actually requires is the guiding principle.

_items.text: Whichever technique is quickest to set up.
_items.feedback: Convenience of set-up does not indicate whether a technique fits the material.

_items.text: Whichever technique was used most recently.
_items.feedback: Recent use has no bearing on whether a technique suits a particular topic.

_items.text: Whichever technique other students on the module prefer.
_items.feedback: Other students' preferences do not determine what a given topic requires.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The choice should follow from what the topic is mainly testing, not from convenience or habit.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think back to what this course has said should drive the choice of technique.
